name: Hindi
variety: Modern Standard Hindi, educated speech of Delhi and western Uttar Pradesh (the variety of Ohala 1999)

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (mean of 5 Urdu speakers from Lahore, stressed monosyllables in a b_l frame); used as a proxy because Hindi and Urdu share one vowel system and no Hindi table could be verified

contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates at five places: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced (p pʰ b bʱ)
dental versus retroflex stops (t̪ : ʈ, d̪ : ɖ)
retroflex flaps /ɽ ɽʱ/ versus retroflex stops /ɖ ɖʱ/ (marginal: the flaps occur only after a vowel) and versus the alveolar tap /ɾ/
phonemic vowel nasalisation on all ten vowels (/saːs/ 'mother-in-law' : /sãːs/ 'breath')
three short lax vowels /ɪ ə ʊ/ against seven long peripheral vowels; length goes together with quality
consonant gemination, word-medial only and only after /ɪ ə ʊ/ (/pət̪aː/ 'address' : /pət̪ːaː/ 'leaf')
/s/ versus /ʃ/; loan fricatives /f z/ are well established, /q x ɣ ʒ/ are kept only by some speakers
allophony: /ə/ is [ɛ] next to /ɦ/ when a consonant or word boundary follows the /ɦ/ (/kəɦnaː/ [kɛɦnaː] 'to say', /ʃəɦər/ [ʃɛɦɛr] 'city'); with /ʊ/ in the next syllable the result is [ɔ] (/bəɦʊt̪/ [bɔɦɔt̪] 'much')
/ʋ/ is [w] as an onglide after a consonant (/pəkʋaːn/) and varies between [ʋ], [v] and [w] elsewhere
/ɦ/ is breathy voiced [ɦ] between voiced sounds, weaker or [h] word-finally; neighbouring vowels are partly breathy
breathy voiced stops have a voiced closure and a breathy voiced release that lasts up to about 100 ms into the vowel, with lowered F0 at vowel onset
nasals are homorganic before stops: /n/ is [m ɳ ɲ ŋ] before labial, retroflex, palatal and velar stops
a nasalised vowel before a voiced stop is often followed by a short homorganic nasal ([tʃãːnd̪] ~ [tʃãːd̪] 'moon'); before a voiceless stop there is none ([d̪ãːt̪] 'tooth')
vowels are phonetically nasalised next to nasal consonants
/ɾ/ is a tap, a trill [r] when geminate or emphatic
stops are unreleased word-finally and before another stop
word-final long vowels tend to be shortened; /ɛː ɔː/ are [əɪ̯ əʊ̯] before /j ʋ/
many speakers replace /q x ɣ z f/ by [k kʰ ɡ dʒ pʰ]
syllable_structure: (C)(C)(C)V(C)(C)(C); the native core is (C)V(C), onset and coda clusters come mainly from Sanskrit, Perso-Arabic and English loans
phonotactics: schwa deletion: the inherent vowel of the script is not pronounced word-finally and is dropped in the context VC_CV (/kəmlaː/ from written kamalā; /nəmkiːn/), subject to morphology and cluster well-formedness
/ɽ ɽʱ ŋ ɳ/ do not occur word-initially
geminates are medial and follow a short vowel; /ɽ ɽʱ ɦ/ do not geminate
aspirated and breathy stops are rare as first members of clusters and deaspirate there
nasal vowels contrast with oral ones in all positions but short nasal vowels are rare

stress.rule: Stress falls on the heaviest syllable of the word (light V, heavy VV or VC, superheavy VVC or VCC) and in a tie on the rightmost non-final one (Kelkar 1968 as analysed by Hayes 1995; Pandey 1989 gives a competing foot-based account).
stress.cues: weak and disputed: Ohala 1986 found no consistent duration or pitch cue; later work reports slightly longer duration and the low target of the phrasal rise (L) on the prominent syllable; no vowel reduction, little intensity difference

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none: unstressed vowels keep their quality; only schwa is short and is deleted in weak positions
rhythm.notes: The class is the usual textbook label; vowel quantity is contrastive and weight matters for prominence. No nPVI value could be verified. Final lengthening has not been measured in a source I can name.

length.notes: Long vowels are roughly 1.7 to 2 times as long as short ones (Urdu stressed monosyllables: long 222-244 ms, short 122-136 ms, Fatima & Aden 2003). Geminate stops have roughly twice the closure duration of singletons.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Lisker & Abramson 1964 (one speaker, word-initial stops in isolated words)
voice_onset_time_ms.notes: VOT does not separate plain voiced from breathy voiced stops (ranges for /ɡ/ -95 to -30, for /ɡʱ/ -160 to -40). The difference lies after the release: noise offset times for velars are k 26, kʰ 74, ɡ 12, ɡʱ 34 ms (Davis 1994), and breathy voicing can last about 100 ms into the vowel (Ladefoged & Maddieson 1996).

intonation.declarative: each non-final content word with its clitics forms a phrase with a rise, low on the prominent (or first) syllable and high at the right edge; the peaks decline through the sentence; the last phrase, usually the verb, is low or falling to a low boundary (L%)
intonation.yes_no_question: same rising phrases, then a high boundary (H%) with the rise on the last syllable of the clause-final verb; the particle kyā is optional
intonation.wh_question: the wh-word stands before the verb and carries focus: expanded rise on the wh-phrase, compressed pitch after it, low boundary
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases; at a clause boundary a higher rise, often with a pause
intonation.accent_shape: L*...H rise per phrase (LH in Harnsberger 1994, L* HP in Patil et al. 2008): low on the prominent syllable, peak on the last syllable of the phrase
intonation.notes: Féry 2010 treats the rises as phrase tones, not word accents. Focus raises and widens the rise of the focused phrase and compresses what follows (Patil et al. 2008). The low target is raised after voiceless and breathy onsets (Khan 2016).

tone.notes: No lexical tone. Breathy voiced stops lower F0 at the onset of the following vowel, which is a phonetic effect only.

phonation: breathy voiced (murmured) stops and affricates /bʱ d̪ʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ/ and flap /ɽʱ/: slack vocal folds, moderately open glottis, breathy release into the vowel
vowels after breathy consonants begin breathy (higher H1-H2, more noise) and return to modal voice within the vowel

problems: Breathy voiced stops (b# d# d.# J# g#) are a modal voiced closure plus an added voiceless aspiration noise sample; the following vowel starts with modal voice and no F0 dip, so bʱ sounds like b followed by h. The IPA output writes them with ʰ (bʰ, dʰ, ɖʰ, ɡʰ, ɟʰ).
/ɦ/ is the voiceless [h] of the base table (phoneme H imports base1/h), never breathy voiced.

The [ɛ] and [ɔ] allophones of schwa next to /ɦ/ are missing for the inherent vowel: पहला, कहना, शहर, बहुत come out as [pʌhəlaː], [kʌhənaː], [ʃʌhəɾ], [bʌhʊt]; the schwa after /ɦ/ is not deleted either. The rule exists only for the independent letter अ.
/ɽʱ/ (ढ़) is produced as the sequence flap + [h] + schwa: पढ़ना gives [pʌɽhənaː] with an extra syllable. The flap phoneme r. has no IPA name and prints as 'r.'.
Schwa deletion is a context rule inside the phoneme definition and fails in words such as हरकत [hʌɾəkət] and उलझन [ʊləɟʰən] (expected [ɦərkət̪], [ʊldʒʱən]).

Candrabindu inside a word gives a nasal vowel plus an alveolar [n] (दाँत [dãnt], चाँद [cãnd]); after an independent vowel or the inherent vowel no nasal vowel is made at all (आँख [aːnkʰ], हँसना [hʌnsənaː]).
The palatal affricates are labelled as palatal stops (IPA c, ɟ); the aspirated c# simply calls the English [tʃ] of the base table, with no separate aspiration phase.
The breathy velar g# carries dental place features in the phoneme table (vcd dnt stp); dentals print as plain t, d in IPA output.
Intonation uses the generic eSpeak tunes: no rising phrase on each content word, and stress is marked by length and amplitude more strongly than in Hindi.
good: dental and retroflex stops are separate phonemes with different transitions
ten oral and ten nasal vowel phonemes, with the long-short pairs differing in quality
gemination is written with the length mark for most stops and lengthens the closure
homorganic nasal from anusvara; loan consonants f z x ɣ q are available
weight-based stress rule (last heaviest syllable, final excluded) matches the literature

notes: The two diphthongs are not phonemes of the Delhi standard: [əɪ̯ əʊ̯] are the realisations of /ɛː ɔː/ before /j ʋ/ and in eastern varieties. In the consonant list /q x ɣ ʒ/ are marginal loan phonemes, /ɳ/ occurs mainly in Sanskrit loans and before retroflex stops, and /æː/ occurs only in English loans. Vowel formants are taken from Urdu speakers and should be replaced when a Hindi table is available.
